lawyer:
Md Imam Hasan, Advocate-For the Petitioner. 
Md Ehsanul Haque, with Md Zobaidur Rahman, Advocates-For the Respondent Nos. 2-5 & 8-9.
parties:
Al-Mamun Mridha ----- Petitioner
Vs.
Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka Metropolitan Dhaka ----- Respondents.
full_judgment:
Md Akram Hossain Chowdhury J : On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution this Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the  respondents to show cause as to why the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed by the respondent No. 1, the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 (Annexure-D) allowing the application of the respondent Nos. 2-5 and 8-9 for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure should not be declared to have been passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 2. At the time of issuance of the rule this Court, pending hearing of rule, stayed the proceedings of Land Survey Tribunal case Nos. 22 of 2008 by an ad-interim order and also passed an order for hearing this rule along with Writ Petition No. 9911 of 2011. But the learned Advocate of the petitioner informed this Court that the rule issued in Writ Petition No. 9911 of 2011 has already been discharged for non-prosecution. In such a position we have taken up this rule for disposal on its own merit. 

 3. The facts leading to the rule, in brief, are that the respondent Nos. 2-7 being plaintiffs filed Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 before the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka under section 145A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 contending inter-alia that an area of 0.0476 acres of land was wrongly recorded in the City Survey Plot No. 3758/3897 instead of 0.0760 acres in the name of respondent No. 2-5 and therefore they filed the above noted Tribunal Case for correction of the record. 

 4. The present petitioner and others being defendants contested the case by filing written statement denying the material allegations made in the plaint and contending inter-alia that the petitioner and respondent No. 15 has been owning and possessing the land in dispute by way of purchase and after scrutinizing the papers and possession the Settlement Officer recorded the land in the name of the petitioner and other respondent in the respective khatian in the last Dhaka City Survey operation. 

 5. During pendency of the Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 the respondent No. 2-5 and 8-9 being applicants filed an application under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for appointment of an Advocate Commissioner for holding a local investigation on the land in dispute. 

 6. The said application was opposed by the present petitioner by filing written objection. The learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal after hearing the said application by his order dated 28-11-2011 allowing the respondents' application for appointment of Advocate Commissioner for holding local investigation under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure and fixed the next date on 8-2-2012 for depositing Advocate Commissioner's fees. 

 7. Since there is no appellate authority appointed as yet under section 145B of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 to challenge any order of the Land Survey Tribunal, the petitioner being aggrieved by the order dated 28-11-2011 by filing this writ petition obtained the present rule along with an ad-interim order staying the proceedings of aforesaid Land Survey Case. 

 9. Mr Md Immam Hasan, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that under section 145D of the statute i.e. the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, empowered the Land Survey Tribunal to exercise its powers following the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure in certain matters, so far as not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act for the purpose of disposal of the land survey case. Though the sub-section (i) (e) of section 145D of the Act, empowered the tribunal for issuing commission but that is to the extent of examination of the witnesses or documents only; other than that particular purpose the tribunal has/had no authority to pass an order for local investigation. The learned Advocate for the petitioner referring to the above section 145D of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 behestly submits that the learned Judge of the Tribunal without applying his judicial mind passed the impugned order in a slipshod manner without assigning any reason thereto. As such, the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 is liable to be declared without lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 11. Heard the learned Advocates, perused the writ petition, affidavit-in-opposition and the annexures annexed thereto. It appears from the record that the respondents, who are the plaintiff Nos. 1-4 and 7-8 in the land survey case has filed an application before the Land Survey Tribunal on 19-7-2009 under Order XXVI, rule 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure for holding a local investigation by an Advocate Commissioner and in the said application they have categorically mentioned in the prayer as to which subjects are to be investigated by an Advocate commissioner in the local investigation; those subjects as mentioned in the application are as follows: 

 145D. Power and Procedure of Tribunals—(i) For the purposes of the disposal of suits or appeals, a Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be, shall exercise the powers and follow the procedure under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, so far as not inconsistent with the provisions of this Act or the rules made there under, in respect of the following matters, namely; 

 (2) Any proceeding before a Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall be deemed to be a judicial proceeding within the meaning of section 193 of the Penal Code. 

 (3) A Land Survey Tribunal or a Land Survey Appellate Tribunal shall sit at such place or places as the Government may fix. 

 (4) The judge of the Land Survey Tribunal or Land Survey Appellate Tribunal may make such administrative arrangements as he considers necessary for the performance of the functions of the Land Survey Tribunal or Land Survey Appellate Tribunal, as the case may be. 

 (5) The Land Survey appellate Tribunal may, of its own motion or upon an application made to it, by order in writing, transfer, at any stage of the proceedings, any suit from the Land Survey Tribunal to another Land Survey Tribunal within the territorial limits of its jurisdiction. 

 17. Thus, we find that the learned Judge of the tribunal upon misconception of law and misreading the materials on record passed a non-speaking order in a slipshod manner which is not maintainable in the eye of law. As such, we are in a considered view that the impugned order dated 28-11-2011 passed by the learned Judge of the Land Survey Tribunal, Dhaka in holding a local investigation in the Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 22 of 2008 was passed without lawful authority and is of no legal effect.
